topic: Burnout and thinking: memory, attention and planning on the return to work
text:
Return-to-work plans after burnout usually focus on hours and energy. Thinking may need a place in them too.

A review of studies comparing people with clinical burnout with healthy comparison groups found they performed somewhat lower on tests of memory, attention and executive function, the skills behind planning and organising. The authors suggest these difficulties be considered when planning a return to work, for example by reducing cognitive demands and alternating complex tasks with simpler ones.

A separate study using remote cognitive testing in people with stress-related disorders found similar modest differences, not at the level of a cognitive impairment diagnosis.

One limit is worth holding: these studies were snapshots, so they cannot show whether the difficulties cause or follow burnout, or how they change over time.

In practice: ask about concentration, memory and planning as well as fatigue, and build a lighter cognitive load into the first weeks back.

Key sources:
Gavelin, H. M., Domellöf, M. E., Åström, E., Nelson, A., Launder, N. H., Stigsdotter Neely, A., & Lampit, A. (2022). Cognitive function in clinical burnout: A systematic review and meta-analysis. Work & Stress. https://doi.org/10.1080/02678373.2021.2002972
Franke Föyen, L., Sennerstam, V., Kontio, E., Lekander, M., Hedman-Lagerlöf, E., & Lindsäter, E. (2023). Objective cognitive functioning in patients with stress-related disorders: A cross-sectional study using remote digital cognitive testing. BMC Psychiatry. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12888-023-05048-5
